Foundations: Making a Product Ready to Scale

Before you make more, you must know your recipe in numbers, know how much your output varies, and prove the bigger batch works. This module teaches scale-up arithmetic with yield and losses, a simple process capability check, and how to lead a pilot run that ends in a clear go or no-go decision.
Scale-up arithmetic: formula percentages, yield and losses
Convert a kitchen recipe into a weighed formula with percentages
Measure the yield of a test batch and use it to plan output
Calculate how much raw material a target order really needs, including losses
Split a large batch into equal loads that fit your equipment

Scaling is not simply "do everything ten times". When you make ten times more, three things change: the **amounts** (which you can calculate), the **losses** (which you must measure), and the **behaviour of the process** (mixing, heating and cooling take longer with more material). This lesson handles the first two with arithmetic. The rest of this module handles the third.
A balance scale
Scaling starts on the scale: every ingredient weighed in grams, never in cups or handfuls.
Step 1: Weigh everything, including eggs and water

Cups, tins and "one small sachet" change from day to day. A digital kitchen scale that reads to 1 g removes that problem. Weigh every ingredient in a good test batch, including liquids and eggs (crack them into a bowl and weigh them). Write the weights down as your **base formula**.
Step 2: Turn weights into percentages

Divide each ingredient weight by the total weight of the mix and multiply by 100. The result is the **formula percentage**. Percentages do not change when the batch size changes, so they are the true identity of your product. If someone in your team says "I added a little more sugar", the percentage shows exactly how far she moved away from the standard.
Step 3: Measure yield, not guess it

**Yield** is how much sellable product you get from what you put in. Weigh the raw mix, then weigh the finished, sellable product after cooking, drying or trimming, and after removing broken or rejected pieces. Yield = sellable output ÷ input × 100. Frying, baking and drying lose water, and some pieces always break or burn, so yield is usually well below 100%. Measure it on at least two or three test batches, because one batch can be lucky.

There is often a second loss after production: spillage at packing, samples for buyers, retained samples for your records, and packs that fail the seal check. Measure this **packing loss** separately so you can see where product disappears.
Step 4: Work backwards from the order
Start with what the buyer wants: number of packs × net weight per pack.
Divide by (1 minus packing loss) to find the finished product you must make.
Divide by the yield to find the raw mix you must prepare.
Divide by your base formula total to get the multiplier, then multiply every ingredient by it.
Round up to whole bags or loads, and write the rounded quantities as the batch sheet.
Worked example: 400 packs of chin-chin from a 1 kg test recipe

For example, Kemi in Ibadan sells chin-chin in 250 g packs. A school has asked for 400 packs for an end-of-term event. Her test batch uses 1,000 g flour, 200 g sugar, 150 g margarine, 100 g egg (2 eggs), 50 g milk powder, 10 g baking powder, 5 g nutmeg, 5 g salt and 180 g water: 1,700 g of dough in total.
Formula percentages: flour 58.82%, sugar 11.76%, water 10.59%, margarine 8.82%, egg 5.88%, milk powder 2.94%, baking powder 0.59%, nutmeg 0.29%, salt 0.29%. They add up to 100%.
Yield: from 1,700 g of dough she got 1,445 g of sellable chin-chin after frying, draining and removing burnt bits. 1,445 ÷ 1,700 = 0.85, so her yield is 85%.
Packing loss measured over three test days: 2%. Order: 400 × 250 g = 100,000 g. Finished product needed: 100,000 ÷ 0.98 = 102,041 g.
Dough needed: 102,041 ÷ 0.85 = 120,048 g. Multiplier: 120,048 ÷ 1,700 = 70.6. Flour needed: 70.6 kg.

Her rented mixer takes up to 10 kg of flour per load, so she rounds up to 72 kg of flour in 8 equal loads of 9 kg. Each load: 9 kg flour, 1.8 kg sugar, 1.35 kg margarine, 0.9 kg egg (about 18 eggs), 0.45 kg milk powder, 90 g baking powder, 45 g nutmeg, 45 g salt, 1.62 kg water.
Check: 72 × 1,700 g = 122.4 kg dough. 122.4 × 0.85 × 0.98 = 101.96 kg sellable, about 407 packs.

Kemi buys and weighs for 72 kg of flour, not the 40 kg she first guessed by "doubling up". Her 8-load plan delivers about 407 packs, so 7 spare packs cover a broken carton or a retained sample from each load.

What arithmetic cannot tell you

Weights scale in a straight line. Processes often do not. A large pot of syrup takes much longer to heat and to cool. A bigger load of dough in a mixer may need more mixing time. A wok overfilled with dough drops the oil temperature and the chin-chin soaks up oil and turns pale. Small amounts of spice and leavening must be weighed on a scale that reads small weights accurately, because an error of a few grams is a big percentage error. This is why the next two lessons measure variation and run a pilot before you accept a big order.
Bigger batches mean bigger hazards

Large quantities of hot oil are dangerous. Keep the fryer on a stable, level surface away from children and walkways, never leave hot oil unattended, keep a fitting lid or fire blanket within reach to smother a fire, and never pour water on burning oil. Lift heavy bags and pots with bent knees or with help. Wash hands and cover hair before handling food, and keep raw eggs away from finished product.
Weigh small ingredients separately
If your main scale reads in 5 g or 10 g steps, buy a small pocket scale that reads to 0.1 g or 1 g for spices, salt and baking powder. Pre-weigh them into labelled small bags before you start mixing.

Is your process steady enough? Measuring variation and capability
Collect 25 or more measurements from a normal production run
Calculate the average, the range and the standard deviation on a phone or spreadsheet
Work out Cp and Cpk and explain what they say about your process
Decide whether to move the target, reduce the spread, or both

No two items are ever exactly the same. Two packs filled by the same person, from the same bowl, a minute apart, will differ by a few grams. That difference is called **variation**. Scaling multiplies variation: if 1 pack in 20 is underweight today, then a 2,000-pack order contains about 100 underweight packs. Before you scale, you need to know how much your process varies and whether it fits inside your specification.

Twenty-five honest measurements tell you more about your process than a hundred good feelings.

Capability: does the spread fit the specification?
Quality engineers compare the spread of a steady process with the width of the specification using two indices, described in the NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods:
**Cp = (USL − LSL) ÷ (6 × s).** It asks: if the process were perfectly centred, would it fit? It ignores where the average sits.
**Cpk = the smaller of (USL − average) ÷ (3 × s) and (average − LSL) ÷ (3 × s).** It asks: given where the average actually sits, how close is the nearer limit?

A Cpk of 1.0 means the nearer limit is exactly 3 standard deviations away; the handbook relates this to about 0.27% of output outside the limits for a normal, in-control process. A Cpk of 1.33 relates to about 64 parts per million.
If Cp is good but Cpk is poor, your spread is fine and your **target** is in the wrong place. If both are poor, you must reduce the **spread**.
Be honest about the sample

The handbook says capability figures are only reliable with large samples, around 50 or more independent values, and only for a process that is stable. With 25 values, treat your Cpk as a first look, not a certificate. Measure items from different times of day and different people, and keep adding data.
Worked example: 1 kg packs of yam flour

For example, Ruth in Oyo packs elubo (yam flour) in 1 kg bags by scooping and topping up. Her specification: never below 1,000 g (the label claim), and not above 1,030 g (more than that gives away too much flour). She weighs 25 bags filled through a normal morning.
Her 25 weights add up to 25,177 g. Average = 25,177 ÷ 25 = 1,007.08 g.
Smallest 1,001 g, largest 1,013 g, so the range is 12 g. Standard deviation from her spreadsheet: 3.21 g.
Cp = (1,030 − 1,000) ÷ (6 × 3.21) = 30 ÷ 19.26 = 1.56. The spread would fit comfortably if it were centred.
Average minus 3 standard deviations = 1,007.08 − 9.63 = 997.45 g, which is below the 1,000 g claim. So some underweight bags are expected even though none appeared in these 25.

Ruth's spread is acceptable (Cp 1.56), but her target sits too close to the lower limit (Cpk 0.74). Moving her target to 1,012 g lifts Cpk to (1,012 − 1,000) ÷ 9.63 = 1.25 at the cost of about 5 g more flour per bag. Reducing her spread with a fixed-volume scoop and a fine top-up spoon is the cheaper long-term fix.

Fix the centre when only Cpk is low; fix the method when the spread itself is too wide.
Ways to reduce spread
Replace judgement with a tool: a fixed-volume scoop, a depositor, a cutting guide, a rolling pin with thickness rings.
Fill most of the weight quickly, then top up on the scale with a small spoon.
Keep the scale on a firm, level table away from fans and vibration, and check it each morning with a known weight.
Train everyone on the same method, then measure each person separately: often one person's technique causes most of the spread.
Never fix underweight by guessing

Selling packs below the declared weight cheats customers and can breach weights and measures and labelling rules. If your data shows a risk of underweight packs, raise the target first, then work on the spread, and only lower the target again when new data proves it is safe.

Leading a pilot run: first-article checks and a go or no-go decision
Write a short pilot plan with clear pass criteria before you start
Brief helpers on roles, safety and what to record
Carry out a first-article check on the first items of a full-size load
Run a debrief and make a documented go, fix or stop decision

A **pilot run** is a full-size batch made under real conditions, with real helpers and real equipment, before you promise anyone volume. It tests the parts of scaling that arithmetic cannot: heat, timing, space, tiredness and teamwork. Your role in a pilot is not to work the hardest. It is to watch, measure and decide.
A person inspecting items with a magnifying glass
In a pilot run, the leader's main tool is careful observation, not extra hands.
Write the pilot plan before the day
**Purpose:** for example, "prove that one 9 kg flour load gives at least 50 sellable packs that meet spec".
**Pass criteria:** written numbers, such as yield at least 83%, no underweight packs in a check of 20, colour matches the reference sample, total time under 4 hours.
**Roles:** who weighs, who mixes, who fries, who packs, who records. One person, often you, only observes and times.
**What to record:** start and end time of each stage, temperatures, weights, problems and changes made.
**Stop rules:** what makes you pause the run, such as oil smoking, a scale reading wrongly, or an ingredient that looks or smells wrong.
First-article check

A **first-article check** means inspecting the first few items of a run against every point of the specification before you make the rest. It catches set-up mistakes, such as a wrong cutting size or a scale set to the wrong unit, while only a handful of items are affected. Check the first items, correct anything needed, record what you changed, and only then let the run continue.
The debrief

Within the same day, sit with your helpers for 15 minutes and ask four questions: What did we plan? What actually happened? Why was there a difference? What will we change next time? Write the answers down. Thank people by name for problems they raised. Helpers who see that reporting a problem is welcomed will keep reporting them when you are not in the room.

Keep the pilot record even when the run fails. A failed pilot with clear notes is valuable: it shows what not to repeat, and later it helps you train new helpers by showing them exactly why each rule in your method exists. File the pilot plan, the record sheet and the debrief notes together under the date.
Worked example: Kemi pilots her 9 kg load

For example, before accepting the 400-pack school order from Lesson 1, Kemi runs three pilot loads of 9 kg flour each on one Saturday with two helpers, Bisi and Tolu. Her pass criteria: yield at least 83%, frying colour matching her reference pack, and all 20 checked packs at 250 g or above.

Load 1: first-article check on the first two wok loads found the dough cut too thick, so pieces were pale inside. She set the cutting guide to the thickness of her test batch and recorded the change. Yield 84%.
Load 2: everything to plan. Yield 86%. All 20 checked packs between 251 g and 258 g.
Load 3: Tolu, rushing to finish, put almost double the usual dough into the wok. The oil temperature dropped, the chin-chin came out pale and oily, and many pieces were rejected. Yield 79%.
Average yield: (84 + 86 + 79) ÷ 3 = 83%, which only just meets the target, and one load failed on its own.
Debrief: the cause of load 3 was no fixed wok load size. Change: a marked bowl holding exactly one wok load of cut dough, and a kitchen timer for each load.

Kemi's decision is "fix and repeat", not "go". She runs two more loads the following week with the marked bowl: yields 85% and 86%. With three loads in a row meeting the criteria (loads 2, 4 and 5), she accepts the order and writes the marked bowl and timer into her method.

Systems, Quality and Operations at Volume

Quality at volume is built into the process, not inspected in at the end. This module turns your method into a control plan with mistake-proofing, teaches sampling and simple control charts so you can watch a process while it runs, and uses takt time and bottleneck analysis to find your true capacity and your true cost per good unit.
A control plan and mistake-proofing for every stage
Identify the few characteristics at each stage that decide final quality
Write a control plan row: what, standard, how, how often, who, and the reaction
Design at least two mistake-proofing devices for your process
Explain the difference between a correction and a reaction plan

When you make 20 items, your eyes and hands catch most problems. When a team makes 2,000, problems slip through unless the process itself is set up to catch them. A **control plan** is a table that lists, for each stage, what must be checked, what "right" looks like, how and how often it is checked, who checks it, and what to do when it is wrong. It is the bridge between your recipe and your batch record.
A clipboard with a checklist
A control plan fits on one page and hangs where the work happens.
Choose the few things that matter

Do not try to check everything. For each stage ask: "If this goes wrong, will the customer notice, or could someone be harmed?" Those are your **critical characteristics**. For a fried snack they include ingredient weights, dough thickness, oil temperature, frying time, cooling before sealing, pack weight and seal strength. For a sewn product they might be cutting size, stitch length and seam strength. For a cream they might be weights, heating temperature and fill weight.

Reaction plan

The **reaction plan** is the column most people forget. A reaction has two parts: the **correction** (what you do with the product already made, such as hold it and re-check) and the **process fix** (what you change so the next items are right, such as adjusting the burner). Writing both in advance means a helper does not have to guess or wait for you.
Worked example: part of Kemi's control plan
For example, after her pilot, Kemi writes a control plan for her chin-chin line and pins it on the wall beside each station.

Weighing: each ingredient against the batch sheet, ±1% for flour, sugar, margarine and water, ±1 g for salt, nutmeg and baking powder. Digital scale. Every load. Weigher signs. Reaction: re-weigh before mixing; if the scale fails its morning check with a 1 kg reference weight, stop and use the backup scale.
Dough thickness: 5 mm, set by rolling pin guide rings. Every sheet. Cutter checks by eye against the guide. Reaction: re-roll the sheet.

Oil temperature: 170 °C, the temperature her pilot proved, measured with a probe thermometer. Before every wok load. Fryer records. Reaction: wait until oil returns to 170 °C before adding dough; if the oil is darkening and foaming, change it and record the change.
Cooling: cool to room temperature, checked by hand on the tray underside. Every tray. Packer. Reaction: wait; warm product sealed in a bag sweats and goes soft.

Pack weight: 250 g minimum. Kitchen scale. 5 packs per load, plus every pack that looks light. Packer records. Reaction: hold the load, check every pack, top up any underweight packs, and tell the supervisor.
Each helper now knows exactly what to check and what to do without asking Kemi. The plan also tells her what columns her batch record needs.
Mistake-proofing: make the wrong way hard

Lean manufacturing calls this **poka-yoke**, a Japanese term meaning "mistake-proofing". The idea is simple: design the work so that the error cannot happen, or is noticed at once. It is cheaper than inspection because it works on every item, every time.
**Pre-weighed kits:** weigh small ingredients for each load into labelled bags the day before. An unused bag left at the end of the day shows something was missed.
**Guides and jigs:** guide rings on a rolling pin, a marked cutting board, a fixed-volume scoop, a bowl marked for exactly one wok load.
**Visual signals:** a red tray for held product, a green tray for passed product. Nothing on a red tray is packed.
**Counters and timers:** a kitchen timer per wok load, or a tally sheet ticked each time a load goes in.
**Shapes that only fit one way:** labelled lids that only fit the right jar size, or separate scoops kept inside each ingredient bucket.
Strongest to weakest quality controls
Error cannot happen (design)
Error stopped at once (device)
Error found at the station
Error found at final inspection
Customer finds the error
Move each check as high up the pyramid as you can; the bottom level is the costliest.

For food products, include the hygiene points from the WHO Five Keys to Safer Food: keep hands, surfaces and equipment clean; keep raw ingredients such as eggs apart from finished product; cook thoroughly; keep food at safe temperatures; and use safe water and raw materials. Write who checks handwashing, hair covering and surface cleaning, and when.
Keep it to one page
If your control plan runs to several pages, nobody will read it at the station. Keep only the critical characteristics, use numbers, and put a photo of the reference product beside it.

Sampling and control charts: watching the process while it runs
Explain what acceptance sampling can and cannot prove
Calculate the chance that a sampling plan accepts a lot with a given defect rate
Set up an individuals control chart with a centre line and control limits
React correctly to signals on a control chart

Checking every single item (100% inspection) is slow and, for some tests such as tasting or breaking a seal, destroys the product. So producers check a **sample**. There are two different jobs for samples: judging a finished lot (acceptance sampling) and watching the process while it runs (control charts). They answer different questions, and confusing them is a common mistake.
A rising line chart
A control chart is simply your measurements plotted in time order, with limits that show what normal looks like.
Acceptance sampling: judging a finished lot

The NIST/SEMATECH handbook describes acceptance sampling as picking a random sample from a lot and deciding what to do with the whole lot from what the sample shows. A **single sampling plan** has two numbers: **n**, how many items to check, and **c**, the most defective items allowed in the sample for the lot to pass. Large buyers sometimes specify their plan using the international standard ISO 2859-1, which indexes plans by an acceptable quality limit (AQL). If a buyer gives you a plan, use theirs and ask them to explain it if needed.

The key lesson is that sampling is a filter with holes. The chance of a lot being accepted depends on how bad it really is. You can calculate this chance with the binomial formula, or with the BINOM.DIST function in Google Sheets or Excel.
Worked example: how often does "check 20, accept if 0 bad" let a bad lot through?
For example, Ruth checks 20 random bags from each lot of yam flour and accepts the lot only if none of the 20 is underweight (n = 20, c = 0). She wants to know how well this protects her.
Chance of accepting = chance that all 20 are good = (1 − defect rate) to the power 20.
If 1% of the lot is underweight: 0.99^20 = 0.818, so the lot passes about 82 times in 100.
If 5% is underweight: 0.95^20 = 0.358, so it still passes about 36 times in 100.
If 10% is underweight: 0.90^20 = 0.122, so it passes about 12 times in 100.

Even a lot with 1 bag in 20 underweight gets through more than a third of the time. Ruth sees that her final check cannot create quality; it can only catch very bad lots. She keeps the check, but relies on her scoop method and her control chart to keep underweight bags from being made.
Control charts: watching the process

A **control chart** shows measurements in time order with a centre line and two **control limits**. The limits come from your own process, not from the specification. They show the range of normal, random variation. A point outside them, or a strange pattern, is a **signal** that something has changed: a new bag of raw material, a tired worker, a scale that has drifted.

The simplest chart for a small producer is the **individuals chart**, where each point is one measurement. NIST gives the limits as the average plus or minus 3 × (average moving range ÷ 1.128). The **moving range** is the difference between each value and the one before it, ignoring the minus sign. Since 3 ÷ 1.128 is about 2.66, a quick rule is: limits = average ± 2.66 × average moving range.
Worked example: Ruth's control chart after improving her method
Total 20,201 g, so the average (centre line) is 20,201 ÷ 20 = 1,010.05 g.
The 19 moving ranges (2, 3, 2, 3, 2, 3, 4, 1, 1, 4, 3, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2, 4, 2, 1) add up to 45 g. Average moving range = 45 ÷ 19 = 2.37 g.
Upper control limit = 1,010.05 + 6.30 = 1,016.35 g. Lower control limit = 1,010.05 − 6.30 = 1,003.75 g.
She draws the three lines on squared paper and plots one bag every 30 minutes from then on.

**One point outside a control limit:** stop, check the last few items, look for what changed (material, person, scale, tool), fix it, and note it on the chart.
**Eight points in a row on one side of the centre line** (one of the Western Electric rules described by NIST): the process average has shifted. Find out why.
**A steady climb or fall:** something is drifting, such as a scoop wearing, oil darkening or a scale battery running low.
**No signal:** leave the process alone. Adjusting a stable process after every small difference adds variation instead of removing it.

Capacity is not how fast your best stage works. It is how fast your slowest stage works. And cost is not what a batch costs divided by what you planned to make. It is what the batch really cost divided by what you could actually sell. This lesson gives you the tools for both.
A stopwatch
Time each stage with a phone stopwatch on a normal day, not your best day.
Takt time: the beat of customer demand

The Lean Enterprise Institute defines **takt time** as available production time divided by customer demand. If you work 480 minutes a day and customers want 240 units a day, you must finish one unit every 2 minutes. Every stage of your process must work at or faster than takt, or orders pile up in front of the slowest stage.
Find the time per unit at each stage

Many small processes work in loads, not single units. Time the whole load, then divide by the number of units the load produces. Time real runs on several days and use the typical figure. Waiting stages such as cooling or curing do not use labour, but they use space and trays, so count those separately.
Worked example: can Kemi supply 2,000 packs a week?

For example, a supermarket and two shops together want 2,000 packs of chin-chin a week from Kemi. Her team works 5 days of 7 hours. One 9 kg flour mixing load gives about 52 packs (15.3 kg dough × 85% yield ÷ 250 g). She times each stage over a week.
Available time: 5 × 7 × 60 = 2,100 minutes. Takt time: 2,100 ÷ 2,000 = 1.05 minutes, or 63 seconds, per pack.
Mixing: 25 minutes per load ÷ 52 packs = 0.48 min per pack. Under takt.
Rolling and cutting by two people: 90 minutes per load ÷ 52 = 1.73 min per pack. Over takt.
Frying: one wok takes 10 minutes per wok load (8 frying, 2 loading and draining) for 2.5 kg of dough, giving 2.125 kg or 8.5 packs. 10 ÷ 8.5 = 1.18 min per pack. Over takt.
Packing and sealing: 0.8 min per pack. Under takt.
The bottleneck is cutting (1.73), not frying as Kemi expected. At 1.73 minutes per pack her line makes only 2,100 ÷ 1.73 = about 1,214 packs a week.

Kemi adds a hand-cranked dough sheeter, which in her trials cuts rolling and cutting to 50 minutes per load (0.96 min per pack), and lights a second wok burner (frying 0.59 min per pack). Cutting is still the slowest stage at 0.96, under takt, so capacity rises to about 2,100 ÷ 0.96 = 2,187 packs a week. She has only about 9% spare, which matters in Module 3.

First-pass yield and cost per good unit

**First-pass yield (FPY)** is the share of units that pass all checks the first time, with no rework. Units that need rework cost extra; scrapped units cost everything and earn nothing. Your real unit cost must include both.
Worked example: cost per good pack

For example, one of Kemi's production days plans 400 packs at a batch cost of about ₦180,000 (approximate, covering ingredients, oil, gas, packaging, labour and a share of rent). Check: 368 + 20 + 12 = 400 packs.
First-pass yield: 368 ÷ 400 = 92%.
Rework cost: 20 packs × about ₦60 for a new bag, label and time = ₦1,200.
Cost per good pack: ₦181,200 ÷ 388 = ₦467, not the ₦450 she gets by dividing ₦180,000 by 400.
The ₦17 gap per pack is the price of poor first-pass yield. Over 2,000 packs a week that is about ₦34,000 a week, which tells Kemi that fixing seal leaks and burning is worth real money.
Do not price from the plan
If you set your selling price from planned output, every defect comes out of your profit. Price from cost per good unit, and update it monthly from your batch records.

Committing to regular supply: utilisation, buffers and honest lead times

Moving from one-off orders to regular supply changes the question. A school order asks "can you make 400 packs by Friday?" A supermarket or distributor asks "can you deliver 300 packs every Monday, for months, whatever happens?" Breaking that promise even once can lose the account. This lesson shows how to decide what you can safely promise.
A delivery truck
Regular supply is a promise that has to survive power cuts, sick days and late deliveries of raw materials.
Use demonstrated capacity, not calculated capacity

Your bottleneck calculation gives a theoretical figure. **Demonstrated capacity** is what you have actually produced, to specification, in a normal week, recorded in your batch records. It is usually lower, because of breaks, cleaning, changeovers and small stoppages. Plan with the demonstrated figure.

To find it, take the last four to eight normal weeks from your batch records, add the packs that passed all checks each week, and use the typical week, not the best one. Leave out weeks with an unusual event such as a festival rush with extra hired help, unless you can repeat that arrangement whenever needed.
Utilisation and the capacity cushion

**Utilisation** = committed weekly demand ÷ demonstrated weekly capacity × 100. At 100% you have no room for anything to go wrong. In real workshops something always goes wrong: a power cut, a helper's child is ill, the flour delivery is late, a load fails its check. When utilisation is very high, one lost day takes weeks to recover, and orders keep arriving while you recover. Keep a **cushion** of spare capacity that you choose deliberately, based on how often you lose time today. Your batch records tell you this.
Worked example: should Kemi accept 500 extra packs a week?

For example, Kemi's batch records show a demonstrated capacity of 2,100 packs a week, or 420 a day over 5 days. She already supplies 1,500 packs a week (WhatsApp orders and two shops). A supermarket asks for 500 packs every Monday.
Current utilisation: 1,500 ÷ 2,100 = 71%. Spare: 600 packs a week.
With the supermarket: 2,000 ÷ 2,100 = 95%. Spare: 100 packs a week.
Her records show she loses about one production day a month to power cuts and illness. One lost day = 420 packs. With 100 spare a week, recovering takes more than 4 weeks.
Counter-offer: 300 packs a week for the first 6 weeks. Total 1,800 ÷ 2,100 = 86%. Spare: 300 a week, so a lost day is recovered in 420 ÷ 300 = 1.4 weeks.
She tells the buyer she will review the volume after 6 weeks of on-time delivery, once her new sheeter has proved itself.

The supermarket accepts 300 packs a week. Kemi delivers every Monday, including the week of a two-day power cut, because her cushion and buffer stock absorb it. After 6 weeks she has evidence to support a larger volume.

A finished-goods buffer

A **buffer** is a small stock of finished, passed product kept back so a bad day does not become a missed delivery. A common starting point is one delivery's worth for each regular customer, then adjust it from your records. Keep the buffer within shelf life: label every carton with its lot code and best-before date, store it cool and dry, and use **first expired, first out (FEFO)**: always deliver the oldest good stock first and move the new production into the buffer.

Handling defects as a team: hold, rework rules and root cause
Set up a hold area and a clear decision for every nonconforming item
Write rework rules that keep rework safe and controlled

At volume, defects are certain. What separates a professional producer is what happens next. If helpers hide defects, mix them back in, or fix them in different ways, your quality becomes unpredictable. If they report them, hold them and follow clear rules, defects become information that makes the process better.
People working together on a puzzle
Root cause work is a team job: the people closest to the work see the causes first.
Step 1: Hold and label

Any item or load that fails a check goes straight to a marked **hold area** (a red tray, a shelf with a red sign) with a tag: product, lot code, what failed, how many, who found it and the time. Nothing leaves the hold area without a decision. This stops suspect product being packed by mistake.

Make the hold rule part of everyone's job from the first day of training: "if in doubt, put it on the red tray and tell me". Thank people when they use it, even when the item turns out to be fine. A helper who is scolded for holding good product will stop holding bad product.
Step 2: Decide, and write the decision
Meaning
Who can decide

Bring it back to specification by an approved method, then re-check
Supervisor, using written rework rules
Downgrade
Sell clearly as a different, cheaper product (for example broken pieces sold as such) if safe and legal
Owner

Destroy so it cannot be sold or eaten by mistake

Accept a minor cosmetic difference that does not affect safety or function

Step 3: Rework rules
Rework only with a written method. Example: a pack with a weak seal is opened, the chin-chin checked, and repacked in a new bag with a new label.
Re-check every reworked item against the full specification, not only the fault that was fixed.
Record rework on the batch record: how many, what was done, who did it.
Set a limit: an item may be reworked once. If it fails again, it is scrapped.
Some faults can never be reworked. For food: anything dropped on the floor, contaminated, past its date, or showing mould is scrapped, never repacked or blended into a new batch.
Never hide a food safety problem

If a defect could make someone ill, such as foreign matter, mould, rancid smell or a cleaning chemical near food, scrap the affected product, check the rest of the lot and the lots made just before and after, and find the cause before restarting. If affected product has already been sold, contact the buyers. Do not repack or relabel to disguise it.
Step 4: Find the biggest problem with a Pareto table

Keep a **defect log**: date, lot code, defect type, quantity. Every two weeks, total each type and sort from largest to smallest. Add a cumulative percentage. Usually a few defect types cause most of the losses. This is called a **Pareto analysis**, and it tells you where to spend your effort.
Worked example: two weeks of defects on the chin-chin line
For example, over two weeks Kemi's team produces about 4,000 packs and logs 100 defective packs: burnt or too dark 46, broken pieces over the limit 30, underweight 12, seal leaks 8, other 4.
Check: 46 + 30 + 12 + 8 + 4 = 100 packs, which is 2.5% of 4,000.
Sort and add cumulative percentages: burnt 46%, then broken 76%, then underweight 88%, then seal leaks 96%, then other 100%.
Two defect types, burnt and broken, cause 76% of all defects.
Kemi chooses "burnt" for the team's first root cause session.
Instead of trying to fix everything, the team focuses on one problem that causes almost half the losses.
Step 5: Fishbone with the team

A **fishbone diagram** (also called an Ishikawa diagram) puts the problem at the head and groups possible causes under bones. Gather the people who do the work for 20 minutes. Ask for causes under each heading, write them all down without arguing, then go and check the most likely ones with data. In Kemi's case the team suggested burner flame too high, thinner pieces from the end of each dough sheet, the timer not reset between loads, and oil not changed on schedule. The defect log showed most burnt packs came from the last wok loads of the day, when the fryer was tired and the oil was oldest.

A **correction** fixes the product in front of you. A **corrective action** removes the cause so the problem does not return. When you sell 50 packs to people you know, a complaint is a conversation. When you sell 2,000 packs a week through shops, a complaint is a search: which packs are affected, what went into them, and where did the others go? **Traceability** answers those questions in minutes instead of days. It also proves to buyers that you run a controlled operation.
Two linked chain rings
Traceability links each pack to its materials and to the customers who received it.
Lot codes

The Codex Alimentarius General Standard for the Labelling of Prepackaged Foods (section 4.6) says each container shall be marked, in code or in clear, to identify the producing factory and the lot. A simple lot code system works for any product: a product letter or two, the production date, and the load number. For example **KC261006-3** means Kemi's Chin-chin, made on 6 October 2026, mixing load 3. Print or stamp it on every pack and carton, next to the best-before date.
The batch record
Your batch record is your control plan turned into a form that is filled in during production. Each load gets one record. It should include:
Lot code, date, product and planned quantity.
Raw materials used, each with the supplier's lot or delivery date ("one step back").
Each control plan check with the actual reading, the time and the initials of the person who checked.
Any deviation from the method, what was done, and who approved it.
Output: units passed first time, reworked, scrapped; yield.
Retained sample taken (yes or no) and where it is stored.
Release: who checked the record and released the lot for sale.
Dispatch: which customer received how many from this lot, and when ("one step forward").
Worked example: tracing a complaint
For example, a shop sends Kemi a WhatsApp photo of a pack that a customer said tasted stale and oily. The pack shows lot code KC261006-3.
She pulls the batch record for KC261006-3. Load 3 of 6 October gave 52 packs. Flour, margarine and oil delivery dates are recorded.
Oil record: the oil was changed before load 1 and not again that day, although her SOP says to change it after a fixed number of wok loads. The fryer's initials show a new helper.
She tastes the retained sample from load 3 and from load 2. Load 3 is stale and oily; load 2 is fine.
Dispatch log: 30 packs of load 3 went to that shop and 22 to WhatsApp customers, all named in her order book.
She replaces the shop's 30 packs, contacts the 22 WhatsApp buyers with an apology and replacement, retrains the helper and adds an oil-change tick box to the batch record.
Within an afternoon Kemi knows exactly which 52 packs were affected and who has them. Without lot codes she would have had to recall a whole week's production or, worse, guess.

Why this matters
Not simply ten times everything
Amounts: you can calculate them
Losses: you must measure them
Process: heat and mixing change
Prove it with a pilot run
When you make ten times more, three things change. The amounts, which you can calculate.
The losses, which you must measure.
And the behaviour of the process. Mixing, heating and cooling take longer with more material.
So in this module you work out your numbers, check how much your output varies, and prove the bigger batch with a pilot run.
Know your recipe
Weights, percentages and yield
Weigh everything, even eggs and water
Formula %: ingredient / total x 100
Yield: sellable / input x 100
Measure packing loss separately
Cups, tins and one small sachet change from day to day. Use a digital scale that reads to 1 g, and weigh every ingredient, including liquids and eggs.
Divide each weight by the total and multiply by 100. These formula percentages do not change with batch size. They are your product's identity.
Yield is how much sellable product you get from what you put in. Frying and baking lose water, and some pieces break or burn, so measure it on two or three test batches. One batch can be lucky.
Then measure packing loss: spillage, samples, and packs that fail the seal check.
Worked example
Kemi: 400 packs of chin-chin
Work backwards from what the buyer receives.
400 x 250 g = 100,000 g of product
Packing loss 2%: make 102,041 g
Yield 85%: prepare 120,048 g dough
Multiplier 70.6: 70.6 kg flour
Round up: 8 loads of 9 kg = 72 kg
For example, Kemi in Ibadan sells chin-chin in 250 g packs. A school wants 400 packs. That is 100,000 g of finished product.
Her packing loss is 2%, so she must make about 102,041 g.
Her measured yield is 85%, so she needs about 120,048 g of dough.
Her test dough weighs 1,700 g, so the multiplier is 70.6. That means 70.6 kg of flour.
Her rented mixer takes up to 10 kg of flour, so she rounds up to 8 equal loads of 9 kg. That gives about 407 packs.
She first guessed 40 kg of flour by doubling up. The arithmetic saved the order.
Safety
Bigger batches, bigger hazards
Stable, level surface. Never unattended. Lid or fire blanket near. Never water on burning oil.
Lift heavy bags and pots with bent knees or with help.
Wash hands and cover hair. Keep raw eggs away from finished product.

Large quantities of hot oil are dangerous. Keep the fryer on a stable, level surface away from children, never leave it unattended, keep a lid or fire blanket near, and never pour water on burning oil.
Lift heavy bags and pots with bent knees, or with help.
Wash hands and cover hair before handling food, and keep raw eggs away from finished product.
Variation
Ruth's 1 kg bags of yam flour
Never fix underweight by guessing. Raise the target first.
Spec: 1,000 g to 1,030 g
25 bags: average 1,007.08 g
Standard deviation: 3.21 g
Cp 1.56: spread is fine
Cpk 0.74: target too close to 1,000 g
No two items are exactly the same. That difference is variation, and scaling multiplies it. For example, Ruth in Oyo packs yam flour in 1 kg bags. Never below 1,000 g, and not above 1,030 g.
She weighs 25 bags from a normal morning. The average is 1,007.08 g.
Her spreadsheet's standard deviation, the typical distance from the average, is 3.21 g.
Cp compares the spread with the specification. Hers is 1.56, so the spread would fit if it were centred.
But Cpk, which checks the nearer limit, is only 0.74. Her target sits too close to 1,000 g, so some underweight bags are expected.
Moving the target to 1,012 g lifts Cpk to 1.25. A fixed-volume scoop and a fine top-up spoon is the cheaper long-term fix. And 25 values is only a first look.

Write the plan before the day
Purpose
Roles: one person only observes
What to record
Stop rules

Give roles. One person, often you, only watches and times.
Record times, temperatures and weights, and agree stop rules, like oil smoking. Then do a first-article check: inspect the first few items against every point before making the rest.

Fix and repeat, not go
What happened
Load 1: dough too thick, 84%
Load 2: all to plan, 86%
Load 3: wok overfilled, 79%
What changed
Cutting guide set and recorded

Remember
Formula percentages are your product's identity
Measure yield and packing loss
Work backwards from packs to flour
Low Cpk: move target; low Cp: reduce spread

Why this matters
Build quality into the process
At 2,000 items, problems slip through
A control plan for every stage
Charts that watch the process
Your bottleneck and real unit cost
When you make 20 items, your eyes catch most problems. When a team makes 2,000, problems slip through unless the process itself catches them.
So first, a control plan with mistake-proofing.
Then a simple control chart that watches the process while it runs.
And finally, your true capacity and your true cost per good unit.
Control plan
Six columns, one page
Characteristic: what we check
Standard: in numbers
Method: which tool or test
Frequency: how often
Who checks and signs
Reaction: fix product and process
Do not check everything. Pick critical characteristics: things the customer will notice, or that could harm someone. For a fried snack, that includes oil temperature, cooling and pack weight.
For each one, write the standard in numbers, the tool, and how often. For example, Kemi checks her oil is at 170 °C with a probe thermometer before every wok load.
Write who checks and signs the record.

The reaction plan is the column people forget. It has two parts: correct the product already made, and fix the process. If a pack is light, Kemi's packer holds the load, checks every pack, tops up, and tells the supervisor.
Keep it to one page, with a photo of the reference product beside it.
Mistake-proofing
Make the wrong way hard
Small ingredients in labelled bags the day before. An unused bag shows something was missed.
Guide rings on a rolling pin, a fixed-volume scoop, a bowl marked for one wok load.
Red tray for held product, green tray for passed. Nothing on a red tray is packed.
Mistake-proofing, called poka-yoke, designs the work so the error cannot happen, or is noticed at once. It works on every item, every time. Pre-weighed kits are one way.
Guides and jigs are another. A rolling pin with guide rings makes every sheet 5 mm.
And visual signals. Nothing on a red tray is ever packed.
For food, add hygiene to the plan: clean hands, surfaces and equipment, raw eggs kept apart, and hair covered. Write who checks, and when.
Sampling
A final check cannot create quality
Ruth checks 20 bags, accepts if 0 bad
1% bad: lot passes about 82 in 100
5% bad: still passes about 36 in 100
Quality must be made, not caught
For example, Ruth checks 20 random bags of yam flour from each lot, and accepts the lot only if none is underweight.
If 1% of the lot is underweight, it still passes about 82 times in 100.
Even at 5% underweight, it passes about 36 times in 100.
Sampling is a filter with holes. So Ruth keeps the check, but relies on her scoop method and a control chart to stop underweight bags being made.
Control chart
Ruth's individuals chart
Control limits come from your data, not the specification.
Weigh 20 bags in filling order
Average: 1,010.05 g
Average moving range: 2.37 g
Limits: average ± 2.66 x 2.37
Plot one bag every 30 minutes
After switching to a fixed scoop, Ruth weighs 20 bags in the order she filled them.
The average, 1,010.05 g, is her centre line.
The moving range is the difference between each bag and the one before. Their average is 2.37 g.
The limits are the average plus or minus 2.66 times that, so 1,003.75 g to 1,016.35 g. Her lower limit now sits above the 1,000 g label claim.
She plots one bag every 30 minutes. One point outside a limit, or eight in a row on one side, means stop and find what changed.
With no signal, leave the process alone. Adjusting after every small difference adds variation.
Takt and bottleneck
Can Kemi make 2,000 packs a week?
Fix the slowest stage first. Buy equipment only for it.
Takt: 2,100 / 2,000 = 1.05 min per pack
Mix 0.48: under takt
Cut 1.73: the bottleneck
Fry 1.18: over takt
Sheeter and second wok: about 2,187
Takt time is available time divided by customer demand. Kemi has 2,100 minutes a week, and shops want 2,000 packs. So one pack every 1.05 minutes.
Time each stage per load, then divide by packs per load. Mixing is 0.48 minutes a pack.
Rolling and cutting is 1.73, the slowest. Not frying, as Kemi expected. Her line makes only about 1,214 packs a week.
Frying, at 1.18, is also over takt.
She adds a hand-cranked dough sheeter and lights a second wok burner. Capacity rises to about 2,187 packs a week.
A faster mixer would not have helped at all.
Worked example
The true cost of a good pack
For example, Kemi plans 400 packs; 368 pass first time, 20 are repacked, 12 are scrapped.
Batch cost for 400 packs
Rework: 20 packs repacked
Naira prices are approximate.
First-pass yield is the share of units that pass every check the first time. Kemi's is 368 out of 400, which is 92%.
Her batch costs about 180,000 naira. Repacking 20 packs adds about 1,200.
That is 181,200 naira for 388 good packs, so 467 naira each, not the 450 she gets from the plan.
Over 2,000 packs a week, that gap is about 34,000 naira. So price from cost per good unit, never from the plan.
Key points
Remember
One-page control plan with reactions
Mistake-proofing beats inspection
Sampling judges a lot; charts watch the process
The bottleneck sets your capacity
Price from cost per good unit
To remember. Write a one-page control plan with reactions. Make errors hard with mistake-proofing. Use charts to watch the process. Fix the bottleneck first. And price from cost per good unit.

Why this matters
Scaling only pays if you keep promises
Promise only what you can deliver
Handle defects without hiding them
Prove where every pack came from
A 90-day plan you can check
A school asks for 400 packs by Friday. A supermarket asks for 300 packs every Monday, for months. Breaking that promise once can lose the account.
At volume, defects are certain. What matters is what happens next.
You must trace any pack back to its materials and forward to its customers.
And you will finish with a 90-day scale-up plan.
Worked example
Should Kemi take 500 more packs a week?
Demonstrated capacity: 2,100 a week
Now: 1,500 packs, 71% utilisation
Plus 500: 95%, only 100 spare
One lost day = 420 packs
Counter-offer 300: 86%, 300 spare
Plan with demonstrated capacity: what you actually produced to specification in a normal week. For Kemi, 2,100 packs a week.
Utilisation is committed demand divided by capacity. She already supplies 1,500 packs, so 71%.
A supermarket wants 500 more every Monday. That is 95%, with only 100 packs spare.
Her records show she loses about one day a month to power cuts and illness. One lost day is 420 packs. With 100 spare, recovery takes more than 4 weeks.
So she offers 300 a week for 6 weeks. That leaves 300 spare, and a lost day is recovered in 1.4 weeks. After 6 weeks of on-time delivery, she has evidence for more.
Buffer and lead times
Promise honestly
Stock buffer
About one delivery per customer
Lot code and best-before on cartons
Cool and dry
Honest lead time
Extra order / spare capacity
Add buying and delivery time
Quote 4 weeks, not 1
Keep a small buffer of passed product so a bad day does not become a missed delivery. Label every carton, and always deliver the oldest good stock first.
For a one-off order, divide it by your spare capacity, then add buying and delivery time. Kemi quotes 4 weeks plus delivery, not 1 week.
And watch long payment terms: waiting 30 days means you fund the stock yourself.
Defects
Hold, decide, rework by the rules
Failed item: red tray, with a tag
Supervisor decides; write it down
Rework by a written method, once
Re-check against the full spec
Dropped, mouldy, contaminated: scrap
Any item that fails a check goes to a marked hold area, with a tag. Nothing leaves without a decision. If in doubt, put it on the red tray, and thank people who use it.
The decision is rework, downgrade, scrap, or use as is, and it is written down.
Rework only by a written method, re-check everything, record it, and allow it only once.
Some food faults can never be reworked. Anything dropped, contaminated, mouldy or past its date is scrapped.
Never hide a food safety problem. Find the cause, and if it was sold, contact the buyers.
Find the cause
Pareto, then fishbone
A correction fixes the product. A corrective action removes the cause.
Two weeks: 100 defective packs
Burnt 46, broken 30: together 76%
Fishbone with the team, 20 minutes
Cause: last loads, oldest oil
Fryer rotation and oil-change rule
Keep a defect log. Over two weeks Kemi's team logs 100 defective packs out of about 4,000.
Sort them largest first. Burnt and broken packs cause 76% of all defects. This is a Pareto table. It shows where to spend your effort.
Then a 20-minute fishbone session: the team lists possible causes under people, equipment, method, materials, measurement and environment.
The defect log shows most burnt packs came from the last loads of the day, when the fryer was tired and the oil oldest.
Her corrective actions: a fryer rotation every two hours, oil changed at a fixed number of loads, and the timer reset written into the method. Two weeks later, she checks the log again.
Traceability
Lot codes and batch records
KC261006-3: Kemi's Chin-chin, 6 October 2026, load 3. On every pack and carton.
Material lots, every check with reading and initials, output, retained sample, release.
Which customer got how many from each lot, and when.
A shop sends Kemi a photo of a pack that tasted stale and oily. The lot code is KC261006-3: chin-chin made on 6 October 2026, mixing load 3.
Her batch record shows the oil was not changed that day, and the fryer was a new helper. The retained sample from load 3 is stale; load 2 is fine.
Her dispatch log shows 30 packs went to the shop and 22 to named WhatsApp customers. Within an afternoon she replaces them, retrains the helper, and adds an oil-change tick box.
90-day plan
Milestones you can check
Days 1-30: pilot and fix the bottleneck
Days 31-60: new volume, three weeks running
Days 61-90: offer proven volume
Budget from two supplier quotes
Move dates, never the quality standard
In the first 30 days, pilot the new load size, trial the bottleneck fix, and train one helper per stage.
By day 60, reach the new volume for at least three weeks in a row, with a control chart running daily.
By day 90, offer the proven volume to a regular buyer, with complete batch records and one trace test passed.
Price each equipment item from at least two suppliers, and review the plan every two weeks. Adjust the dates, never the quality standard.
Key points
Remember
Plan with demonstrated capacity
Keep a cushion and a buffer
Hold failed items; rework once, by rules
Pareto first, then fishbone
Lot code on every pack and carton
To remember. Promise from demonstrated capacity, with a cushion and a buffer. Hold failed items and follow rework rules. Remove causes with Pareto and fishbone. And put a lot code on every pack.
